report:
### Conclusion
No, high-quality scientific evidence demonstrates that **hydroxychloroquine does not reduce the likelihood of dying from COVID-19**. Major clinical studies show that it offers no mortality benefit and may even be associated with increased mortality.

### Key Evidence

* **Large Randomized Controlled Trials:** Major international platform trials, including the UK’s RECOVERY trial and the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Solidarity trial, evaluated hydroxychloroquine in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Both trials concluded that the drug produced little to no reduction in mortality compared to standard care, leading to the immediate halt of hydroxychloroquine trial arms (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine).
* **Collaborative Meta-Analyses:** A meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials analyzing both published and unpublished data found that hydroxychloroquine treatment for COVID-19 was associated with an increased risk of mortality (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z).
* **Regulatory Action:** The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) revoked its Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for hydroxychloroquine to treat hospitalized COVID-19 patients after determining that clinical trial evidence indicated it was unlikely to be effective and that its potential benefits did not outweigh its risks (https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/coronavirus-covid-19-update-fda-revokes-emergency-use-authorization-chloroquine-and).
* **Clinical Practice Guidelines:** Major medical consensus bodies, such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) COVID-19 Treatment Guidelines Panel, recommend against the use of hydroxychloroquine for the treatment of COVID-19 in both hospitalized and nonhospitalized patients (https://dason.medicine.duke.edu/sites/default/files/nih_covid-19_treatment_guideline_updates_8-28-20.pdf).
